title: Robots Colliding on a Rail
statement:
Robots sit on a straight rail. Robot i starts at positions[i], has healths[i] hit points and moves in direction directions[i]: 'L' toward smaller positions or 'R' toward larger ones. All robots start at the same moment and move at the same speed. Positions are distinct, and they are not given in sorted order.

When two robots meet, the one with less health is destroyed and the other loses exactly 1 health and keeps going in its direction. If both have the same health, both are destroyed. Robots moving the same way never meet.

Return the health of every robot still alive after all collisions, listed in the order the robots appear in the input (not by position). Return an empty array if none survive.

examples.why: The robot at 9 first meets the one at 4 and wins (health 6), then meets the one at 1 and wins again (health 5).
The robots at 5 and 8 meet with equal health and both are destroyed. The robot at 2 never meets anyone.
The robot at 1 beats the one at 5 (health 5), then loses to the one at 9 (health 6), which escapes to the left. Output follows input order: index 2, then index 3.

hints: Only a robot moving right followed (by position) by a robot moving left can ever meet. Sort the robots by position first.
Scan from left to right. A left-moving robot fights the right-movers to its left, nearest first. Which data structure gives you the nearest one, then the next nearest?
Push right-movers on a stack. For a left-mover, fight the top of the stack until one side is gone: pop the loser, take 1 health from the winner. If the stack empties, the left-mover survives.

explain.intuition:
This is the bracket-matching idea in disguise. After sorting by position, a right-mover is like an open bracket waiting for a partner, and a left-mover is a closing bracket that cancels the nearest open one before it. The nearest unfinished right-mover is always the most recent one seen, so a stack holds exactly the robots that are still waiting to be hit.

A left-mover keeps fighting the top of the stack. If it loses, it stops. If it wins, it loses 1 health and fights the next one. If it empties the stack, nothing to its left moves toward it any more, so it survives. Right-movers left on the stack at the end also survive. Because the answer must follow the input order, store healths by original index and read the survivors off in that order at the end.
steps: Sort the indexes 0..n−1 by position. Copy healths into a mutable array h.
Walk the sorted indexes. For a right-mover, push its index on the stack.

For a left-mover i, while the stack is not empty and h[i] > 0: compare with the top j. If h[j] < h[i], set h[j] = 0, pop, and decrement h[i]. If h[j] > h[i], decrement h[j] and set h[i] = 0. If equal, set both to 0 and pop.
Return h[i] for every original index i with h[i] > 0, in index order.
pitfalls: Processing robots in input order instead of position order. The second and third examples give different answers if you do.
Returning survivors in position order. The answer must follow the input indexes.
Forgetting that the winner loses 1 health, so a winner can lose the next fight it would have won.

complexity.time: O(n log n) for the sort; the stack pass is O(n)

solutions.title: Simulate one collision at a time
solutions.idea: Keep the living robots in position order. Repeatedly find a neighbouring pair moving toward each other, resolve that fight, and remove the dead.

solutions.title: Sort by position, stack of right-movers
solutions.idea: Right-movers wait on a stack. Each left-mover fights the stack top until it dies or the stack is empty.

followups: Also report the time of each collision if the robots move one unit per second. Which collisions happen first?
Robots now have different speeds. Does the stack approach still work? Why not?
